hook: Many older adults find smartwatch charts baffling, yet they already trust a jade bracelet to tell them how their health is doing.
lede: In the Shanghai parks where the team studied older adults at exercise, wrists carried bangles and bracelets, even a red band printed with “secret text”. Smart wearables are a different story: only 7% of their users are 65 or older, and small screens, dense metrics and well-meant large fonts leave many confused or feeling marked as old. LIFEELING starts from the object older adults already trust and the belief that comes with it: that exercise “detoxes” the body, and a lustrous jade bracelet means health is improving. The result is a bracelet concept that speaks in light and gentle vibration instead of numbers.

chapters.title: Charts that confuse, fonts that feel old
paragraphs: Wearables turn the body into data, and for many older users that is exactly the problem. In experiments with older adults using Sony wristwatches, Nike’s Fuel points alongside steps, distance, sleep, calories and activities left some participants confused. Small buttons, cramped screens and aging eyes make the numbers harder still.

The usual fix, larger fonts and simplified colors, brings its own cost. Research on these “age-friendly” designs finds a pervasive sense of shame: a big-print display is easier to read, but it overlooks the fear of being seen as old.

quote.text: I can’t read much of the data from those smartwatches, I just want to know if I’m exercising enough and if I’m healthy.

chapters.title: A bracelet that already means something
paragraphs: After eight hours of observation in a park, the team interviewed five older adults, aged 65 to 73, in depth. Alongside a wish for simpler signals, one theme stood out: a relationship with objects. Influenced by Buddhist culture, some older people treat particular items as safeguards for their health, and in China jade bracelets are regarded as talismans: when the jade is smooth and lustrous, its wearer’s health is thought to be improving too.

That belief sits alongside another widely held idea, that exercise “detoxes” the body, promoting the smooth flow of vital energy and bodily fluids. Together they suggested a different kind of interface: not a screen to be read, but an object whose appearance changes as health does.

quote.text: I was in average health before, but when I went to Tibet as a volunteer two years ago, a Buddhist guru gifted me two bracelets, which I have been wearing every day since then, and I feel that my physical health has improved significantly and my athletic vigor has increased.

figures.caption: In the park: bracelets worn during exercise, the “secret text” on one of them, and a woman attempting a difficult movement.

chapters.title: From dark green to flowing light
paragraphs: The interviews also showed that these exercisers value a challenge: they felt difficult exercise built confidence and health. Auntie Wang recalled straining her shoulder when she first practiced one hard movement, then practicing until it gradually got better and she could do many more. What they wanted was guidance that keeps a challenge from turning into an injury.

LIFEELING answers with three functions: “Detox” reminds wearers to move, “Flow of life” rewards them while they exercise, and “Alarm” steps in with breathing guidance. Shaped to mimic the aura of jade, the ring would carry an ECG sensor facing the hand, a band of light and a vibration engine, all planned around a flexible circuit board. Four states tell the story:
points: Too little exercise: after a long inactive stretch the ring turns dark green, “toxins” waiting to be cleared
Exercising: orange-yellow, pulsing with heart rate and breathing
Over-exercising: deep red, a vibration every three seconds and a breathing light that pulses twenty times a minute, fading back to light green once breathing settles

figures.caption: The ring’s four states, from dark green through flowing light green and orange to twinkling red.

chapters.title: Room for a little mystery
paragraphs: In a second park, 20 people aged 60 and over, 11 of whom already wore a bracelet, saw a prototype alongside images and a concept video. Most accepted the idea and the form. “The design of this device is very intuitive; I quickly learned how to use it,” said two of them; others called it modern and practical. The jade look was particularly popular with older women.

The detox metaphor was the part people wanted more of. Some hoped different colors could show the body’s detox state; P4 said seeing their health status made them “feel more at ease”. Others asked for exercise records over months so they could adjust their routines. And some wanted the opposite of a clear readout.

quote.text: I would like some symbols with ambiguous meanings; they make me feel more empowered.

takeaways: For older users, a familiar belief can carry health information without a chart: color on a bracelet they already trust needs no decoding.
Designing from cultural meaning, rather than bigger fonts, offers a way around the stigma that “age-friendly” interfaces can carry.
The authors see room to extend metaphor design to other health, smart-home and education devices, drawing on local concepts such as yin-yang balance and qigong.
